content:
I have been a loyal fan and customer of Sonos for a long time, dating back to the original Sonos One. So around two years ago, when I heard Sonos was entering the over-ear headphones market, I knew I had to give it a try. The Sonos Ace looks great, feels comfortable to wear, and brings some excellent Sonos ecosystem features. However, as a pair of high-end headphones, there are still several areas that left me feeling it fell short—for instance, the bass wasn't strong enough, the active noise cancellation (ANC) could be better, and the app experience needed improvement. But now, the new Sonos Ace Ultra seems to address almost every complaint I and most customers have had, one by one. I have been using them as my daily go-to headphones for nearly a month—travelling, editing videos, working out, walking around, and for everyday music listening—so I have a thorough understanding of them. Here's what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our Sonos Ace Ultra hands-on video review below:

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra doesn't look much different from the original Sonos Ace. Sonos has kept the same sleek, understated design, only slightly adjusting the placement of the chrome accents and adding a few more colours. But the biggest differences actually lie inside the headphones.

The differences between the original Sonos Ace and the Ultra

Here are the biggest changes upgrading from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

  • Redesigned 40mm drivers
  • Upgraded microphone array from 8 to 10
  • Improved adaptive noise cancellation, claimed to be up to twice as effective, with automatic adjustments for glasses, hair, and changes in earcup seal
  • Longer battery life—up to 35 hours with ANC on
  • Bluetooth 6.0 (previous version had 5.4)
  • More robust EQ options, offering three presets and an advanced 8-band EQ
  • Headphones can be connected to the Sonos ecosystem
  • User-replaceable battery
  • Updated cushioning materials on the earcups and headband
  • Earcups rotate to a greater angle and can lay flat when worn around the neck
  • Two new colours: Agave Green and Sand

Of these changes, the ones I felt most noticeably were the redesigned acoustic architecture, stronger bass performance, and more powerful ANC. When using the original Sonos Ace, I would occasionally hear a hissing sound in ANC mode. Although it was rare, I definitely noticed it. So far, the new Sonos Ace Ultra has resolved this issue. Some of the great specs from the previous generation have also been retained, including:

  • Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos
  • Dynamic head tracking
  • Lossless audio support on compatible devices
  • USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio inputs
  • Bluetooth multipoint connection
  • Fast charging: 3 minutes of charging delivers up to 3 hours of playback
  • TV Audio Swap functionality with compatible Sonos soundbars

The headphones carry over the same high-quality build, combining plastic and metal materials for a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also retains the magnetic replaceable earcups, and personally my favourite addition is the new EQ settings, which really let me fine-tune the sound to my liking. But as everyday-use headphones, how do they actually perform?

My experience using them

I'll say it again: specs on paper are easy to write down, but the biggest reason I truly love the Ace Ultra is that the sound quality has noticeably improved. The biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was that the bass lacked depth. The bass itself wasn't bad, but for a pair of $450 headphones, I felt it always fell short. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop music, so bass is very important to me. I wanted stronger low-end punch—to feel the impact of the bass. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience I wanted.

The low-end impact and weight have noticeably improved. But what's worth noting is that Sonos didn't simply turn up the bass. Any brand knows how to boost the bass, but the difficulty lies in preserving layering so the bass doesn't drown out the vocals, instruments, and highs. It's precisely this that drew me deeply to the Ace Ultra. The bass is stronger, yet the vocals remain clear, bright, and pleasant. It's not just for music—everything from podcasts, movies, and all the YouTube videos I watch sounds great, performing impressively across different media playback scenarios.

The improved ANC is also immediately noticeable the moment you switch it on. The new 10-microphone array allows more sounds to be dynamically isolated. Even when nothing is playing, the headphones are astonishingly quiet in many different environments—almost too good! The biggest improvement in the ANC is in handling sudden noises. Isolating consistent noise (like an aircraft engine) is one thing; isolating passing vehicles, construction sites, sirens, or sudden loud sounds when out walking is another—and the Ace Ultra excels in this area.

Finally, I want to mention two points: wearing comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These are the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn. Even on 8- to 10-hour flights, I had them on about 95% of the time without any soreness or discomfort. Lastly, I have many Sonos speakers at home, and they added a new feature that lets you switch music from the speakers to the headphones with one tap. This feature is great, but personally I don't use it much.

My only complaint is that the carrying case needs a new zipper or closure design, because the stickers keep sticking to it!

Pricing and availability

The Sonos Ace Ultra goes on sale today on the Sonos website and Amazon, priced at $449—the same as the original Sonos Ace's launch price. Available in four colours: Black, White, Agave Green, and Sand. I've also noticed the original Sonos Ace is on sale on Amazon for $239, while stocks last. At the $240 price point, that could also be a decent option.

At a $450 price point, the Sonos Ace Ultra firmly holds its own in the high-end noise-cancelling headphones market, competing head-on with products from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Conclusion

The original Sonos Ace felt like a decent first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete, refined product. As we've seen, Sonos didn't redesign the exterior, but improved every important aspect and added several impressive new features. The sound quality is noticeably better, the ANC is stronger and smarter, the battery life is longer, the app experience is smoother, and the Agave Green colour is genuinely gorgeous.

If you already own the original Sonos Ace, I think this upgrade is worthwhile, depending on what you value. If you're in the market for a pair of high-end headphones, I believe the Sonos Ace Ultra deserves a place on your shortlist. At $449, it's certainly not cheap, but if you want a pair of top-tier premium headphones and you're a Sonos fan, you'll definitely love them.

What do you think? Have you tried the Sonos Ace lineup? Are you a Sonos customer? What's your take on the app experience? Let's discuss in the comments below!
